caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Guinea's debt was reset by HIPC completion in 2012: from 95.2% of GDP in 2006 it fell to 26.9% by 2012, the series low. The post-relief government borrowed for mining-linked infrastructure, and the ratio climbed back to 48.0% projected for 2025, roughly double the post-HIPC low but still moderate. The Simandou iron ore megaproject and bauxite boom have transformed the fiscal outlook, with revenues rising strongly. Sustainability is comfortable if mining revenues are managed well; the risk is the familiar one of spending the boom before it arrives, compounded by political instability that has repeatedly interrupted IMF programs.
inflation_management: Guinea's inflation was tamed over the period, falling from a series high of 34.7% in 2006 to a projected 3.1% in 2025, the series low. The early-2000s money-printing era gave way to tighter central bank policy and, after 2010, IMF-supported stabilization: inflation fell from 21.4% (2011) to single digits by 2014 and stayed there, even through Ebola (2014-16) and COVID. The 2022 global shock produced only 10.5%, easing steadily since. The Guinean franc floats with management, and while there is no formal inflation target, the central bank's restraint since 2011 has been the quiet success of Guinea's macro story.

key_events.event: Conté died; military coup; 2009 stadium massacre killed protesters.
Alpha Condé won the first democratic election; HIPC completion cut debt to 26.9% of GDP.
Ebola epidemic devastated the economy and health system.
Condé won a disputed third term after a constitutional change; mining boom accelerated.
September 2021: military ousted Condé; Colonel Doumbouya took power.
Simandou iron ore project advanced toward production; bauxite exports boomed.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is a mining-driven boom: Simandou and bauxite could make Guinea one of Africa's fastest-growing economies, with debt sustainable and inflation low. Upside is transformational if revenues are invested; downside is the resource curse plus political risk, a return to the instability that has wasted previous windfalls. Uncertainty is high: the economics are excellent, the politics are the variable.
